## Conclusion

The claim that ibuprofen worsens COVID-19 infection is **not supported by evidence** and is considered largely debunked.

The scare originated in March 2020 when French Health Minister Olivier Véran tweeted a warning based on a speculative hypothesis (published as correspondence in *The Lancet*) that NSAIDs might upregulate ACE2 receptors, theoretically aiding viral entry (sciencealert.com). The World Health Organization initially advised caution but quickly reversed course, stating it found "no evidence of severe adverse effects" from ibuprofen use in COVID-19 patients (cbc.ca).

Subsequent, more rigorous research has consistently failed to find harm. A large cohort study of over 38,000 hospitalized COVID-19 patients found NSAID use was "not associated with increased COVID-19 severity, all-cause mortality, invasive ventilation, AKI, or ECMO"—and some analyses even showed associations with better outcomes (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9107579/, link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12985-022-01813-2). A systematic review in *PLOS/Wiley* similarly concluded that "data did not suggest that exposure to NSAIDs increases the risk of having SARS-CoV-2 infection or increases the severity of COVID-19 disease," though it noted study limitations warranting further research (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8426976/). A 2021 study in *The Lancet Rheumatology* likewise reported it "complements several previous observational studies, of which most have supported the lack of association between NSAID use and COVID-19 severity" (thelancet.com/journals/lanrhe/article/PIIS2665-9913(21)00144-2/fulltext).

**Bottom line:** While early theoretical concerns prompted caution, the weight of clinical evidence shows ibuprofen does not worsen COVID-19 outcomes. Major health bodies including the WHO have walked back initial warnings, and both patients and clinicians may reasonably use ibuprofen for symptom relief unless other medical contraindications exist.
